pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Classifying Materials

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-1):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]." Clarification: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]." DCI PS1.A: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]." SEP: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations. CCC: Patterns.

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Working Scientifically, LKS2 Y3/4):** No specific content statement, but the enquiry type is statutory: "gathering, recording, classifying and presenting data in a variety of ways to help in answering questions" and "identifying differences, similarities or changes related to simple scientific ideas and processes." Builds on the KS1 'compare and group' objective and feeds the Y5 comparative/fair-test work.

- **Operational details:** This is the step up from casual sorting to a planned investigation. Have children choose ONE observable property to test (e.g. flexibility, hardness, magnetism), decide how they will test it the same way for every material, TEST several materials systematically, record each result in a table, and only THEN classify by the pattern of results. The discipline is consistency: the same test applied to every material, and the classification driven by recorded evidence rather than a first impression. Surface the Patterns crosscutting concept — which materials share the property? — and revisit that the same set classifies differently under a different property. Keep the property observable/testable at this age (not conductivity or solubility yet, which come in Y4–Y5).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (procedural). The child can plan a simple consistent test for one property, carry it out across several materials, record results in a table, and classify the materials into groups justified by the recorded evidence — recognising the shared-property pattern.
bestPractices: Insist on ONE chosen property tested the SAME way for every material — consistency is what makes it an investigation rather than casual sorting.
Record each result in a table BEFORE classifying, so groups are driven by evidence not first impressions.
Make the Patterns concept explicit: ask which materials share the property and name the group by the shared property.
Revisit rule-dependence — re-run with a different property and watch the same materials regroup — reinforcing that classification depends on the criterion.
Keep properties observable and testable for the age (hardness, flexibility, magnetism, texture); defer conductivity/solubility to Y4–Y5.
Model the plan→test→record→classify sequence so children internalise the investigation structure, not just the outcome.
keyRepresentations: A results table (materials down the side, the tested property across the top)
Sorting rings/branching (Carroll or simple tree) filled FROM the recorded results
A 'shared property' pattern highlight (which materials clustered together and why)
A re-classify prompt: the same materials sorted under a second property
commonMisconceptions: Classifying by an untested surface feature (colour, size) or first impression rather than by a systematically tested property.
Applying the test inconsistently across materials, so the comparison and resulting classes are invalid.
Treating classification as a fixed property of the object, not realising the groups depend on the chosen criterion.
Skipping the record-then-classify discipline — grouping from memory or expectation instead of from the data table.
Confusing 'classify' (assign to groups by a rule) with merely 'describe' or with running a fair test for a purpose (a different enquiry type).

learn.summary: For 7–8 year olds learning to classify materials by observable properties, the core objective is a planned investigation (not casual sorting): choose ONE observable property, apply the SAME test to each material, record every result in a table, and only then classify from the recorded evidence — surfacing the pattern of which materials share the property, and seeing the same set regroup under a different property. The primary approach is a hands-on (or on-screen) investigation bench with live results logging; supporting approaches check the procedure with ordering/matching tasks and an annotated worked investigation.

activities.title: Investigation bench: pick a property, test the same way, record, then classify
feedback: If a group does not match the recorded table, highlight the mismatched material and ask the learner to re-check their own result before regrouping.

When a learner predicts or records 'yes' for a non-magnetic metal (aluminium foil, a piece of copper pipe or wire), have them slowly bring the magnet and watch nothing happen: the recorded 'no' is the fact — not all metals are magnetic. Only a few metals, such as iron, nickel and most steels, are attracted (some stainless steels are not). If a 'copper' coin sticks to the magnet, accept that result too: many such coins are copper-plated steel.
If the test is applied differently to different items, reset to one fixed testing action and have them repeat it identically on every material.
After a 'switch property' re-sort, prompt: 'The same materials, different groups — what changed? The materials, or the question we asked?'
Highlight the shared-property cluster and ask the learner to name the group by the property it shares.
activities.rationale: The target skill is procedural and multi-step: plan → test → record → classify. Live state can enforce the discipline (same test for all; classify from the record) and stage the re-classify-by-a-new-property realisation, making the criterion-dependence of classification concrete. A physical tray and magnet give a parallel hands-on enactment of the same procedure.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-PS1-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]'; clarification color/texture/hardness/flexibility and shared-property patterns; DCI PS1.A; CCC Patterns.
DfE KS2 Working Scientifically (LKS2): 'gathering, recording, classifying and presenting data in a variety of ways'; 'identifying differences, similarities or changes'.
Classification misconceptions: sorting by untested surface features, inconsistent testing, treating class as fixed rather than criterion-dependent.
learnerActions: Choose ONE observable property to test (e.g. 'is it magnetic?', hardness, or flexibility) from an offered set of age-appropriate, testable properties.
Commit to a single fixed test action and apply it identically to every material in turn (e.g. bring the same magnet to each material the same way).

Record each result as it happens in a table with materials down the side and the tested property across the top — e.g. steel paperclip yes, piece of copper pipe or wire no, wooden peg no, steel key yes. (Avoid using a coin as the 'copper' example: many 'copper' coins, such as UK 1p and 2p coins made since 1992, are copper-plated steel and are attracted to a magnet.)
Only after the table is complete, sort the materials into groups (e.g. 'magnetic' / 'not magnetic') and check that each group matches the recorded data.

Press a 'switch property' option to re-test the exact same materials under a second property (e.g. hardness) and watch them regroup — e.g. the steel key and a glass marble now share a group they did not before.
Name the shared-property group: say which materials clustered together and why.
Pair the screen work with a real tray of materials and a magnet to carry out the physical investigation alongside.
activities.intendedInsight: A classification is not a fixed fact about a material; it is the answer to the particular question you chose to test. Consistency of the test and grouping from recorded evidence (not first impressions) are what make it an investigation.

activities.title: Spot the flaw and order the steps (procedure checks)
feedback: For the inconsistent-test item, point to exactly which material was tested differently and why that invalidates the comparison.
For a wrong grouping, show the row in the table that contradicts the chosen group.
If the step order is wrong, emphasise that recording must come before classifying so groups are driven by evidence, not memory.
activities.rationale: Ordering and matching tasks can check whether a learner recognises the procedure and detects an invalid (inconsistent) test. Use as a check or reinforcement; such a task does not itself let the learner generate the evidence, so pair it with the investigation.
sourceClaims: Classification misconceptions: sorting by untested surface features, inconsistent testing, treating class as fixed rather than criterion-dependent.
learnerActions: Put the stages of a classifying investigation into the correct order: plan the test → test each material the same way → record results in a table → classify from the results.
Given a short scenario, identify an inconsistent (unfair) test used within a classification — where one material was tested differently from the others.
Given a completed results table, pick the classification (grouping) that genuinely matches the recorded data.
Sort stated materials into groups by a named property.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising the correct investigation sequence, consistent testing, and evidence-matching groups reinforces the structure of the skill — though recognising it is not the same as carrying it out.

activities.title: Walk through a completed investigation (annotated model)
feedback: When a learner reveals a group, confirm whether their stated reason matches the recorded evidence for that group.
After the re-sort flap, ask which materials swapped groups and why, to check they attribute the change to the chosen property, not the materials.
If the learner treats the groups as fixed, point back to the second grouping as a counter-example.
activities.rationale: A guided annotated example reinforces the investigation structure and the shared-property pattern. It is a worked model that supports — but does not itself provide — the learner conducting and recording their own test.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-PS1-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]'; clarification color/texture/hardness/flexibility and shared-property patterns; DCI PS1.A; CCC Patterns.
learnerActions: Examine a finished investigation showing the results table, the groups formed, and the shared-property pattern.
Reveal the reasoning behind each part: tap the table, the single test method, and each group to see why the materials were placed there.
Open a flap/panel that re-sorts the same materials under a second property and compare the two groupings.
Explain in your own words why the same materials ended up in different groups.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing a fully worked, correctly structured investigation can make the plan→test→record→classify sequence and the criterion-dependence of groups explicit before or after doing one yourself.

constraints: Keep properties observable and testable at this age (hardness, flexibility, magnetism, texture); defer conductivity and solubility to later years (Y4–Y5).
Insist on ONE chosen property tested the SAME way for every material; consistency is what distinguishes an investigation from casual sorting.
Require recording in a table BEFORE classifying, so groups are driven by evidence rather than first impressions.

Correct the specific misconception 'all metals are magnetic': aluminium and copper are metals but are not attracted to a magnet, and a recorded 'no' must be accepted even when it contradicts expectation. Only ferromagnetic materials (e.g. iron, nickel, cobalt and most steels) are noticeably attracted. Some stainless steels are not, and some 'copper' coins are copper-plated steel and are attracted. Do not let learners override a tested result in either direction.
Distinguish 'classify' (assign to groups by a rule) from merely 'describe', and from running a fair test for a purpose (a different enquiry type).

Ordering/matching tasks and annotated worked examples can check or reinforce the procedure but do not themselves elicit the learner planning and running the test that generates the evidence; use them alongside, not instead of, an actual investigation.

An in-role dialogue does not itself supply the physical testing or a populated data table, and children this age are unlikely to drive such an open conversation to a valid classification; keep the activity grounded in doing and recording.

Because classifying by observable properties is not inherently spatial, a clean 2D bench is sufficient and a real tray gives genuine tactile enactment; a 3D model's depth/physics offer no particular spatial affordance this classification task requires and add handling overhead.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated or tested interventions.

Self-audit of the magnetism example: the source row's correct-answer and probe content correctly treat aluminium and copper as non-magnetic metals and steel paperclip/steel key as magnetic — this is accurate (ferromagnetism). The 'all metals are magnetic' belief is flagged as a misconception to correct, not propagated, and the activity feedback explicitly resolves it rather than only caveating it.

One source (STEM Learning misconceptions) is marked unverified (verified:false) in the row; claims about specific misconception patterns rest on it. Treated as a supporting principle, not as evidence that any activity here was tested.
'Switch property' re-sort and shared-property highlight are retained as concrete interaction examples of the learning mechanism, offered as options, not mandated implementations.
Medium-limitation statements for conversation and 3D are retained only as narrow observable affordances / age-suitability notes, not as categorical claims that those media cannot teach the procedure.

probeDeeper: Your chart says the aluminium foil isn't magnetic even though it's metal — does that surprise you? What does it tell us?
Did you test every material in exactly the same way?
If we chose a different property instead of magnetism, would the groups be the same?
Is this copper coin magnetic? Test it — were you right beforehand?
assess.correctAnswer: Brings the magnet to each material the same way, records a yes/no for each in a chart, and sorts into magnetic / non-magnetic groups strictly from the recorded results — finding that only the steel paperclip is attracted, and that the other metals (aluminium, copper) are NOT.

errorPatterns.pattern: Classifies from assumption, not results — 'all metals are magnetic', so groups metals together without genuinely testing, or overrides a 'no' from the aluminium.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have them slowly bring the magnet to the aluminium foil and copper coin and watch nothing happen; the recorded 'no' is the fact — not all metals are magnetic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Records or predicts 'yes' for a non-magnetic metal without a real test, or dismisses the actual result.

errorPatterns.pattern: Inconsistent test or no record — tests each material differently, or keeps results in their head, so the grouping can't be justified.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold a record-as-you-go chart and one fixed testing action; this is a procedure gap — reconnect to grouping-by-property rather than reteaching magnetism.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No chart; groups produced from memory or feel; the magnet is used differently on different items.

errorPatterns.pattern: Tests several properties at once — muddles 'magnetic' with 'shiny' or 'heavy' and sorts by a blend.
errorPatterns.nextMove: 'One property at a time' — fix the single test (does the magnet pull it?) before sorting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Groupings track shininess/weight as much as magnetism.

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by assumption or appearance without a consistent test or any record.
responseLevels.full: Applies one consistent test to every material, records results in a chart, and classifies strictly from the recorded data — accepting a result that contradicts expectation.
responseLevels.partial: Runs a test and records some results, but lets prior belief (all metals are magnetic) override a surprising result, or applies the test unevenly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out five materials (steel paperclip, aluminium foil, copper coin, plastic counter, wooden bead) and a magnet. Say: 'Plan and carry out a test to find which are magnetic. Test each the same way, record what you find in a chart, then sort them into groups from your results.' Watch them plan, test and record.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The aluminium and copper cases are deliberate traps for 'all metals are magnetic'. Watching shows whether the grouping is DRIVEN by the recorded test results or by assumption, whether the test is applied consistently, and whether results are actually recorded rather than remembered.
